explanations: terra: Israel is commanded to remember God's favor, beginning an account in which the next verses identify liberation from Pharaoh as the content of that favor.
terra: God's rescue of Israel from Pharaoh's household and its brutal oppression specifies the emancipating favor recalled in 2:47.
terra: The Israelites ransom captives while also expelling and attacking their own people; the verse exposes the contradiction between an unbinding payment and conduct that recreates subjection.
terra: Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God, locating the retained value of generosity in divine keeping instead of the recipient's obligation.

luna: This account of righteousness joins giving wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, petitioners, and freeing people from bondage (وفي الرقاب), uniting the section's open hand and its image of manumission. | terra: Righteousness includes giving loved wealth and spending it فِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, so the generous hand directly becomes a means of emancipation.

luna: The section's dictionary branch for wrongful reaching means taking what one has no right to; this verse forbids consuming others' wealth falsely and using judges to seize it, giving that grasping hand a specific legal form.
terra: One person sells himself seeking God's approval, using a commercial transfer to describe freedom from ordinary human return.

luna: The verse forbids taking back what was given to a wife, with a stated exception when she gives compensation to secure release from the marriage; it marks the specific boundary between a gift and a negotiated return.
terra: A party entitled to half a bridal payment may waive it, and both are told not to forget graciousness, showing a legal claim released without erasing generosity.

luna: The section frees its donor from repaying any person's favor; this ayah uses the debt image for a good loan to God (يقرض الله قرضا حسنا), whose return comes from God rather than a human beneficiary. | terra: The good loan to God turns a creditor's world inside out: wealth leaves the human hand and God, who needs no loan, multiplies its return.

luna: The command to spend comes before a day with no sale or friendship (لا بيع فيه ولا خلة); as in the section, wealth's human exchange value cannot help at the final reckoning. | terra: Believers must spend before a day with no trade, friendship, or intercession, placing the gift beyond ordinary exchange and social repayment.

luna: Allah is the believers' Wali and brings them from darkness into light; this makes the section's patron word an active liberating relation, not a human claim to repayment. | terra: God as the believers' protecting ally brings them from darkness to light, supplying a liberating act for the section's benefactor-patron branch of ولى.

luna: The section's giver parts with wealth for God's sake; this ayah stages spending as seed that multiplies many times, showing how a gift's consequence may exceed the amount given. | terra: The seed multiplied seven hundredfold depicts God, rather than the human recipient, supplying the increase returned for expenditure.

luna: After giving, these people do not follow their spending with reminders or injury (منا ولا أذى); the section's freed giver likewise does not turn a gift into a debt collectible from its recipient. | terra: Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminder or injury refuse to turn their helping hand into a later claim on its recipient.

luna: Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury (صدقة يتبعها أذى); this sets a gracious response against a gift turned into leverage, as in the section's no-debt giver. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, clarifying the human relation protected by 2:262 and prohibited in 2:264.

luna: This ayah warns against nullifying charity by reminders and injury (بالمن والأذى); it shows the human claim that the section's giver has no need to collect from beneficiaries. | terra: The command not to nullify charity with reminder and injury shows the section's benefaction becoming an instrument of debt and domination.
terra: Spending for God's approval is pictured as a fruitful garden, giving a positive form to the section's gift free of human claims.
terra: The question about a garden destroyed when its elderly owner and dependents most need it continues the spending passage with another image of worldly provision suddenly leaving the hand empty.

luna: This command concerns what people give from their earnings and crops, warning them not to select what they themselves would reject; it makes the quality of the giving hand part of the image. | terra: Givers must offer good things and not what they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, making receiver and giver meet under one standard.
luna: Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this names the fear of scarcity that closes the hand and contrasts it with trust in the giver's bounty.

luna: The ayah says public charity is good and concealing it while giving to the poor is better; this makes visible and hidden forms of the section's giving hand legible. | terra: Open charity is good but concealed charity to the poor is better and removes sins, protecting the gift from display and from social leverage over its recipient.

luna: This ayah says charity is spent seeking God's face (ابتغاء وجه الله), the same motive the section assigns to its giver, and locates the gift's purpose beyond settling a human claim. | terra: Spending is expressly for God's face, while every good expenditure is repaid to the giver; this transfers repayment from the human recipient to God.

luna: This ayah identifies needy people who cannot travel for livelihood and do not persistently ask others; it helps the reader see that the section's asking hand belongs to real need, not an abstract word. | terra: The restrained poor do not ask people importunately and may be mistaken for self-sufficient, refining the section's image of the outstretched begging palm.

luna: Those who spend their wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, are promised reward; the verse makes explicit that the hand's giving is not confined to one occasion or manner. | terra: Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, have their reward with their Lord, placing recompense outside the beneficiary's debt.

luna: This ayah contrasts God's increase of charity (يربي الصدقات) with the erasure of usury, distinguishing a gift from wealth put to work for a financial return. | terra: God destroys usury and causes charities to grow, opposing extraction from debt to the fruitful gift that relinquishes a claim.
terra: Believers are ordered to relinquish outstanding usury, naming the creditor's surrender of excess immediately before 2:279 limits collection to principal.
terra: Creditors who abandon usury retain only their principal and must neither wrong nor be wronged, setting the boundary immediately before the hardship rule of 2:280.

luna: The section's cited ع س ر dictionary branch describes demanding a debt from an insolvent person without waiting for ease; this ayah sets the boundary in the opposite direction, ordering delay until ease and saying waiving the debt as charity is better. | terra: A debtor in hardship must receive respite until ease, and remission as charity is better; this directly reverses the dictionary's harsh creditor who refuses to wait for ميسرة.

luna: The section describes a world of actual debts and claims; this verse concerns a real debt for a fixed term and orders it written fairly, helping distinguish a contractual liability from the section's freely given wealth. | terra: The command to record a deferred debt and its term supplies the ordinary creditor-debtor world from which charitable remission and divine repayment depart.

luna: The section's dictionary image treats blessing as a hand; this prayer locates all good in God's hand (بيدك الخير) and says He gives and withholds rule, framing the ultimate giver. | terra: God gives and removes dominion, honors and abases, and all good is in His hand; giving, taking, benefit, and the hand meet explicitly here.
terra: Divine bounty is said to be in God's hand and He يُؤْتِيهِ to whom He wills, joining hand, favor, and giving in one formulation.

luna: The section identifies sadaqa as wealth a person gives; this ayah says righteousness requires spending from what one loves, making the gift a real relinquishment rather than payment for a prior favor. | terra: One does not reach true goodness until spending what one loves, giving specificity to a hand that parts with what it could tightly keep.
luna: The righteous spend in both ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people; this joins the section's giving hand with a response that releases a claim rather than demanding its return.
terra: God, rather than hostile human powers, is the believers' patron and the best helper, another direct Quranic location of true mawlāship.

luna: The section's miser keeps a hand closed; here what they withhold is made into a collar around their necks, turning the closed hand into a burden. | terra: What people withheld in stinginess will be placed around their necks, turning retained wealth into the bodily bond described in the prose.

luna: Guardians are told to hand orphans their property and not substitute bad for good or consume it; this gives the section's rightful giving and wrongful reaching an exact setting of entrusted wealth.
luna: The women are to receive their marriage-gifts as a gracious giving, and may remit some only willingly; this separates a freely ceded gift from an amount a recipient is forced to return.

luna: Guardians must return orphans' wealth when they are ready and may not consume it wastefully or hastily; the verse distinguishes a rightful handover from a custodian's attempt to take what is not his.
luna: Those who consume orphans' property unjustly are warned they consume fire; this is a concrete instance of the section's dictionary sense of reaching for what is not rightfully yours.
luna: The verse forbids restricting wives in order to take back part of what was given to them; it shows a prior gift being turned into a claim against its recipient.
luna: Even a great amount given to a wife may not be taken back when a husband replaces her; this is a direct boundary against treating a gift as a recoverable debt.
luna: The verse invokes the solemn covenant between spouses as the reason taking back the gift is grave; it completes 4:20's direct prohibition with the relationship that makes the return a betrayal.

luna: The section distinguishes a rightful gift from taking what is not one's right; this verse forbids wrongful appropriation but permits trade by mutual consent, marking the boundary between a grasping hand and a lawful exchange.
terra: The command to do good includes those whom one's right hands possess, requiring beneficence precisely within the master-dependent relation developed by the section.

luna: The verse describes misers who hide what God gave them of His bounty; it links the section's closed hand with concealing a gift whose source lies beyond the recipient. | terra: The verse joins stinginess, urging it on others, and concealing what God gave from His bounty, contrasting the received divine hand with the withheld human one.

luna: The verse criticizes people who spend their wealth to be seen by others; this distinguishes the section's giver seeking God's face from a hand opened for public credit. | terra: Spending merely to be seen makes human spectators the intended return, contrasting with giving solely for God's face.
terra: The following question asks what loss there would be in believing and spending from God's provision, restoring the divine source obscured in 4:38.
terra: A greeting must be answered with one better or equal, providing a bounded form of human reciprocity that clarifies what the section's uncollectable gift leaves behind.

luna: For accidental killing, this ayah requires freeing a believing slave and sets blood compensation for the family unless they waive it; release, compensation, and waived claim meet in one ruling. | terra: The verse repeatedly joins freeing a believing slave with blood compensation, while allowing the victim's family to remit its monetary claim as charity.
terra: Secret counsel is good when it commands charity or reconciliation, and seeking God's approval moves its great reward away from human beneficiaries.
terra: God restrains the hands of a people who intended to stretch them against the believers, a hostile form of the section's reaching hand.
terra: Israel's covenant joins zakat and a good loan to God, placing giving inside fidelity to God rather than a claim upon beneficiaries.
terra: Moses asks Israel to remember God's favor in making them a free, endowed people, another divine-benefaction frame for the community rescued from servitude.
terra: Abel refuses to stretch his hand to kill even if Cain stretches his, setting an ethical boundary on the hand's power to reach and seize.
luna: The verse says that even all the earth's wealth could not ransom those facing punishment; it gives a concrete limit to the section's claim that wealth cannot save its owner at the fall.

luna: In the law of retaliation, waiving a claim is called charity (فمن تصدق به); the section's gift-without-debt image gains a concrete case where a person gives up an enforceable return. | terra: One entitled to retaliation may relinquish it as charity, turning a claim that could be collected into release and expiation.

luna: The verse answers the claim that God's hand is chained by saying His hands are spread wide and He gives as He wills; this extends the section's tight and open hand image to the contrast between a human giver and the unbounded divine giver. | terra: The claim that God's hand is fettered is answered with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ and His free spending, making open and bound hands figures of bounty and stinginess.

luna: Among the expiations for a broken oath is freeing a slave; this is another specific instance of release as an act that discharges an obligation. | terra: Freeing a slave is one of the concrete expiations for a broken oath, so wealth or ownership becomes a hand that unbinds another.
luna: The ayah says no offered compensation will be accepted from the soul facing judgment; it extends the section's warning that wealth cannot buy release at the end.
terra: The Messenger asks no human wage for the reminder, paralleling the giver who seeks no human repayment for a benefit conveyed.
terra: Giving the harvest's due while forbidding waste joins an acknowledged claim of the needy to measured release from one's produce.
terra: A good deed receives tenfold recompense while an evil deed receives only its equivalent, distinguishing God's generous two-way جزاء from strict human equivalence.
terra: Moses says that God favored Israel above others, naming the true benefactor immediately before another retelling of their release from Pharaoh.
terra: Rescue from Pharaoh's people and their killing of sons supplies the concrete liberation behind the favor named in 7:140.

luna: If people turn away, this verse names Allah as their Mawla; it brings together the section's turning-away verb and its dictionary branch for a patron or benefactor. | terra: If opponents turn away, believers are reminded that God is their patron, the best patron and helper, joining تولي with the true source of protection.
terra: Captives are promised that God may give them better than what was taken from them, reversing loss and custody through divine giving.
terra: Payment of tribute عَن يَدٍ stages a hand transferring wealth under subjection, unlike the section's free gift that seeks no mastery.

luna: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way embody the section's closed hand; the next ayah describes the consequence, while this one identifies the withheld wealth. | terra: Hoarded gold and silver that are not spent in God's way embody wealth held tight instead of released.
terra: The hoarded wealth of 9:34 is heated and branded onto foreheads, sides, and backs, making retained property become a bodily bond and punishment.
terra: People pleased only when given a share of alms and angry when denied embody the receiving hand governed by expected benefit.
terra: Contentment with what God and His Messenger give would release the demand displayed in 9:58 and redirect hope toward God.

luna: This distribution of alms includes freeing people from bondage (وفي الرقاب), showing charity itself directed to the section's image of slavery and release. | terra: The prescribed uses of alms include both freeing necks and debtors, placing the section's slavery and debt scenes inside one act of giving.

luna: The hypocrites are described as holding their hands back; this makes the section's miser's closed hand a concrete act of withholding, tied to forgetting God. | terra: The hypocrites قَبَضُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ, a literalized withdrawal of their hands that stages the section's miserly closed palm.

luna: These people vow that if God gives them bounty they will give charity; 9:76 shows that after receiving it they withhold it, so this row supplies the promise that the neighboring reversal breaks. | terra: The promise to give charity if God grants bounty sets truthfulness at the point where received gift should become a giving hand.

luna: After God gives them of His bounty, these people become stingy and turn away (بخلوا به وتولوا); the paired roots named in the section make this a direct reversal of giving and its freedom from a claimant. | terra: After God gives them from His bounty, they become stingy and turn away; بَخِلُوا and تَوَلَّوا unite two of surah 92's roots in one failed response to a gift.

luna: This ayah says hypocrisy was placed in their hearts because they broke their promise to God and lied; following 9:76's stingy turning away, it shows the consequence of the failed pledge. | terra: Their broken promise and lying explain why the stinginess and turning of 9:76 are also a failure of صدق, joining truth and almsgiving branches of the root.
terra: Some Bedouins treat what they spend as a financial loss and wait for disaster to reverse their position, the interested calculation opposed to pure giving.
terra: Others treat spending as a means of nearness to God and the Messenger's prayers, relocating the gift's aim from human repayment to God.

luna: The section's cited dictionary sense defines sadaqa as what one gives from one's self and wealth; here alms are taken from wealth to purify the giver, tying the gift to purification. | terra: Taking charity from wealth is said to purify and increase its givers, directly paralleling giving wealth in order to purify oneself.
terra: God is the one who accepts charities, identifying the ultimate receiver of a gift whose needy human recipient is not made liable for repayment.

luna: This ayah depicts God as purchasing the believers' lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise; it clarifies the section's giving for God's face as an exchange with God, not repayment to a human benefactor. | terra: God buys believers' lives and wealth for the Garden, turning the whole debt-and-sale world into a covenant whose counterparty is God.
terra: Every expenditure is recorded so God may repay them with the best of what they did, making divine record the giver's source of return.
terra: Noah asks no reward from his people and places his reward with God, the prophetic form of acting without a human claim.
terra: Noah asks his hearers for no wealth because his reward lies only with God, directly separating conveyed benefit from payment.
terra: Hud asks no reward and identifies his Creator as the one who rewards him, again refusing the beneficiary's debt.
terra: Joseph's brothers arrive with poor merchandise and ask him to complete the measure and give charity, staging the requesting hand before one able to give.
terra: The Prophet asks no reward for the reminder, so the addressed people are not made debtors for receiving it.
luna: The praised people spend from what God provided, both secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; this pairs the section's gift with a response that does not keep score.
terra: Moses names God's favor in rescuing Israel from Pharaoh's people and their brutal subjection, presenting liberation itself as divine نِعْمَة.

luna: This ayah commands spending from God's provision before the day with no trade or friendship; it repeats 2:254's final deadline while linking it directly to provision and giving. | terra: Secret and public spending must precede the day when neither trade nor friendship remains, another limit on treating generosity as a worldly transaction.

luna: The section's dictionary entry names نعمة as a hand or benefaction; this ayah says every blessing people have comes from God, shifting the source of the “hand” away from a human creditor. | terra: Every favor possessed by people is declared to be from God, displacing the human benefactor's claim to be the originating hand.

luna: The verse pictures those given more provision refusing to share it with people their right hands possess; that unequal hand relation illuminates the section's link between wealth, ownership, and bondage. | terra: Those favored in provision refuse to pass it to people their right hands possess so that they become equal; the verse exposes mastery maintained through a withheld gift.
terra: The parable opposes an owned slave who can do nothing to one whom God provided well and who spends secretly and openly, making freedom visible as the power to give.
terra: People recognize God's favor and then deny it, a specific failure to acknowledge the originating giver rather than a debt owed to a human intermediary.
terra: Every person's record is fastened to the neck, bringing the section's debt garment and neck-bound withheld wealth into the scene of final accounting.
terra: The person must read his own record and suffice as accountant, specifying the collection and reckoning implied by the neck-bound record of 17:13.
terra: Giving relatives, the poor, and travelers their due begins the expenditure unit whose bodily rule is the hand of 17:29.
terra: The condemnation of squanderers defines one excess surrounding the fully outspread hand in 17:29.
terra: Even when one must turn a petitioner away while awaiting provision, one must speak gently, governing the moment an empty hand cannot give before 17:29 states its limits.

luna: The section sets giving against the miser's withholding; this image says not to bind the hand to the neck or open it without limit, giving the reader both edges and the measured hand between them. | terra: The hand chained to the neck and the hand spread to its utmost are the Quran's bodily limits for the section's clenched and extended palm.
terra: Humans would withhold even God's treasuries out of fear of spending, explicitly naming إِمْسَاك as the reflex behind the tight fist.

luna: The section says wealth will not help the one who falls; the ruined garden owner turns both palms over what he spent, making the image of the empty hand after loss. | terra: The ruined garden owner turns his empty palms over what he spent, the concrete image of a giving hand left with nothing when its worldly attachment collapses.
terra: After the garden owner's empty-handed regret, no party can help him against God and he cannot defend himself, removing the human patronage on which worldly benefit might rely.
terra: The ruined-garden scene concludes that true protection belongs to God and that He gives the better reward and outcome, relocating both patronage and recompense.
terra: Everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant, joining the root's coming sense to the section's slave relation in one eschatological scene.
terra: Each person comes to God alone, completing 19:93 by stripping the arriving servant of every human patron and account.
terra: Every soul is to be recompensed for what it strives, placing the section's سعي and جزاء together in a single divine accounting.
terra: God tells Moses that He had already conferred favor on him, opening the divine account that undercuts Pharaoh's later claim to be Moses' benefactor.
terra: Moses is cast into the chest, taken by God's and his enemy, given love, and raised under God's eye; this identifies the agency inside the upbringing Pharaoh later claims.
terra: The return to Moses' mother, rescue after the killing, and years of trial complete God's account of care, sharply limiting Pharaoh's alleged debt.
terra: God is the one who gave every thing its created form and then guided it, extending the section's giving hand to creaturely fitness and direction.
terra: Recipients of sacrificial food include the contented and the one who asks, bringing the giving hand and two postures of need into a single distribution.
terra: Sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God; only piety reaches Him, marking the boundary that prevents an offering from becoming a material payment to God.
terra: God is called the believers' مَوْلَى and the best patron and helper, locating true protective mastery in God rather than a human benefactor's claim.
terra: Those who give what they give while fearing their return to God display a giving hand anxious about acceptance rather than human repayment.
terra: The question whether the Messenger asks a wage is answered by the Lord's better reward, moving recompense away from human recipients.
terra: People of means are told not to stop supporting relatives and the poor after an offense but to pardon, preventing a benefaction from becoming retaliatory leverage.

luna: For slaves seeking a written contract, the verse orders the contract and then says to give them from God's wealth (وآتوهم من مال الله); it joins the section's slave's work toward freedom with an actual transfer of wealth. | terra: A contracted slave seeking freedom is to be contracted with and given وَءَاتُوهُم from the wealth God gave the owners, joining emancipatory striving, God's prior gift, and a liberating human hand.
terra: The Prophet asks no wage except that a person choose a path to the Lord, making the recipient's own return to God the only requested response.

luna: The servants' spending is neither excessive nor miserly but balanced; this states the middle measure between the two hand positions set out in the section. | terra: The faithful spend neither wastefully nor niggardly, locating the measured hand between the two bodily extremes of 17:29.

luna: Pharaoh invokes having raised Moses as a child among them (ألم نربك فينا وليدا), a concrete example of the favor a giver may later hold over its recipient; 26:22 supplies Moses' answer. | terra: Pharaoh cites raising Moses as a child as a benefit now chargeable against him, opening the precise conversation in which nurture becomes debt.
terra: Pharaoh adds Moses' past deed and calls him ungrateful, showing the creditor's accusation that converts former care into a claim; 26:18 supplies the claimed care.
terra: Moses says his Lord granted him judgment and made him a messenger after his flight, supplying a divine gift beside Pharaoh's claimed benefit in 26:18-22.

luna: The section says a human favor can become a debt that binds; Moses answers Pharaoh's claim of nurture by naming the enslavement of the Israelites, exposing the coercion behind that claimed favor. | terra: Moses calls the claimed upbringing a نِعْمَةٌ Pharaoh holds over him and sets it against Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel, joining favor, reminder, and slavery explicitly.
luna: On the Day when neither wealth nor children avail, the section's warning about wealth failing at the end is stated directly.

luna: The next ayah says only one who comes to God with a sound heart is saved; it supplies the inward condition against which 26:88's useless wealth is measured, recalling the section's giving to purify oneself.
terra: Noah's repeated declaration that his reward rests only with the Lord supplies the no-human-payment stance in the same surah as Pharaoh's favor claim.
terra: Hud likewise asks no human wage and leaves recompense with the Lord.
terra: Salih likewise refuses human wage for the benefit of his warning.
terra: Lot likewise places his reward with the Lord rather than his addressees.
terra: Shuayb likewise refuses human wage, completing the surah's repeated boundary against turning guidance into a payable favor.
luna: The queen says she will send Solomon a gift and see what the envoys return; the next ayah reveals the gift's transactional test, meeting the section's image of a hand that expects repayment.

luna: Solomon rejects the queen's gift and says what God gave him is better (فما آتاني الله خير مما آتاكم); the human gift cannot bind him to a return, clarifying the section's distinction between God's bounty and an indebted hand.
terra: The powerful jinn says he will bring the throne before Solomon rises, giving a concrete Quranic scene for the section's secondary sense of ءتى as bringing rather than giving.

luna: The section notes that the root ء ت ي can mean giving and also bringing something; the knowledgeable one says he will bring the throne to Solomon, joining gift-like transfer to physical arrival. | terra: The person with knowledge brings the throne before Solomon's glance returns, intensifying the bringing sense introduced in 27:39 and distinguishing it from monetary giving.
terra: Pharaoh's household picks up the infant Moses who will become their enemy, beginning the ironic history behind Pharaoh's later claim of nurture.
terra: Pharaoh's wife asks that the infant not be killed and proposes adopting him, specifying the household care later presented as a collectable favor.
terra: God prevents other nurses and Moses' sister leads the household back to his own family, limiting Pharaoh's ownership of the benefit he claims.
terra: God returns Moses to his mother so that she is consoled, identifying divine restoration as the hidden agency within his upbringing.
terra: The command to do good as God has done good to the addressee turns received benefit into onward beneficence rather than a claim against recipients.
terra: One who brings good receives better than it, whereas evil is repaid only according to the deed, contrasting generous and equivalent forms of divine recompense.
terra: The analogy asks whether owners make their slaves equal partners in their provision, using the feared collapse of mastery to expose a boundary in human giving.
terra: Giving the relative, poor person, and traveler their right is declared best for those seeking God's face, preparing the contrast with interested increase in 30:39.

luna: The verse contrasts usury, which does not increase with God, with zakat given seeking God's face; that distinction sharpens the section's separation of charitable giving from a human debt or claim. | terra: The verse contrasts a gift intended to grow in other people's wealth with zakat intended for God's face, precisely separating interested transfer from unindebted giving.

luna: The verse says God and the Prophet both bestowed favor on Zayd (أنعم الله عليه وأنعمت عليه); though its immediate issue is his marriage, it recalls the section's former slave whose relation to his benefactors is described through favor. | terra: Zayd is the person whom God favored and the Prophet favored, preserving within one clause the human and divine favor attached to a formerly enslaved man.

luna: This ayah says whatever is spent, God replaces it and is the best provider; it makes God's provision, rather than repayment from the human recipient, the giver's horizon. | terra: Whatever is spent is replaced by God, identifying the true source of recompense when the recipient owes the giver nothing.
terra: Whatever wage the Prophet might have asked is declared to be for the people themselves, while his actual reward is with God.
terra: No one can withhold mercy God opens and no one can release what He withholds, placing the open and closed hand ultimately under divine rule.
terra: Humans are the poor before God and God is the self-sufficient, establishing why no human gift can make God a debtor.

luna: These worshippers spend from what God provided and hope for a trade that will not fail (تجارة لن تبور); their spiritual return clarifies the section's giver's relation to God. | terra: Secret and public spending is called a commerce that will never perish, relocating the transaction from a beneficiary's debt to an account with God.

luna: The next ayah says God will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty; it supplies the divine return behind 35:29's unperishing trade. | terra: God pays the givers' rewards in full and adds from His bounty, completing the unperishing commerce named in 35:29.
terra: The city is told to follow messengers who ask no wage, treating freedom from a payable favor as a sign of trustworthy guidance.
terra: Disbelievers refuse the command to spend from God's provision and ask why they should feed someone God could feed, a verbal closure of the hand.
terra: God's favor to Moses and Aaron introduces another account of the true benefactor behind release from Pharaoh.
terra: God rescues the brothers and their people from great distress, specifying the liberating content of the favor announced in 37:114.
terra: The Prophet says he asks no wage and is not fabricating a role, joining lack of payment to sincerity.
terra: A slave disputed by several masters is contrasted with one belonging wholly to one man, clarifying how mastery itself divides or settles a dependent life.

luna: The verse says an evil is repaid only with its like, while a believing doer of good receives more than a simple worldly balance; it develops the section's two directions of recompense. | terra: Evil is recompensed only with its like while righteous action receives entry into provision without account, another explicit boundary between the two directions of recompense.
terra: The stated exception to asking a wage, affection for kin, is a specific boundary to the otherwise repeated no-wage stance, though its relation to material repayment is indirect.

luna: The section's root ج ز ي includes answering good and evil; this ayah makes the boundary explicit, with an evil repaid in kind but forgiveness rewarded by God, beyond a human debt claim. | terra: An evil may be repaid only with its like, while pardon and reconciliation move reward to God; this states both reciprocity and its merciful boundary.
terra: On judgment day no patron can avail another patron, dissolving the human networks of protection and payable favor imagined by the section.
terra: After captives are secured, the command permits gracious release or ransom, placing unbinding and payment at the two ends of captivity.

luna: The verse calls Allah the Mawla of believers and says disbelievers have no Mawla; it gives the section's patron and benefactor word a divine referent beyond a human bond of indebtedness. | terra: God is the patron of believers while disbelievers have no patron, clarifying the Quranic boundary around the section's benefactor-master sense of mawlā.
terra: Were people pressed for their wealth, they would become stingy; the pressure of an exacting claimant elicits the section's clenched hand.

luna: When believers are asked to spend, the stingy are told their withholding harms themselves and that God is rich while they are needy; this reverses the section's open hand and self-sufficient miser. | terra: When summoned to spend, the miser harms only himself because God is rich and people are poor, exposing the closed hand's false self-sufficiency.
terra: God's hand above the hands of those pledging stages a hand that binds covenant rather than gives; it may illuminate the section's wider movement from hand to obligation.
terra: People treat their submission as a favor owed by the Messenger, but the verse reverses the claim: God is the one who conferred the favor of guidance.

luna: A due share in the wealthy person's property is assigned to the petitioner and deprived person; this gives the asking hand in the section a recognized place in the giver's wealth. | terra: Their wealth contains a right for the asker and the deprived, again treating giving as delivery of another's right rather than creation of a debt.
terra: God wants neither provision nor feeding from creatures, closing off the idea that human giving supplies a divine need.
terra: God Himself is the provider of firm power, completing 51:57's reversal of giver and recipient.
terra: The question whether the Prophet asks a wage so that people are burdened by debt makes explicit the oppressive account his mission does not create.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for ج ز ي includes repayment for good and evil; this verse says God repays those who do wrong and those who do good, specifying both sides of that meaning. | terra: God recompenses evil by what was done and good with the best, setting both directions of جزاء under His just and generous measure.
terra: أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰ stages a hand that gives a little and then stops, a direct boundary case for the section's giving motion.
terra: A human has only what he strives for, which recalls the slave's سعاية labor toward release while placing ownership in one's work rather than another's favor.
terra: The striving of 53:39 will be seen, making the labor toward freedom and every other striving subject to divine witness rather than a human master's account.
terra: That striving is then repaid with the fullest recompense, directly joining سعي and جزاء across 53:39-41.
terra: The camel's killer فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ, using the section's secondary تعاطي motion for a wrongful reaching that culminates in seizure and violence.

luna: The section notes the root ج ز ي for recompense in both good and evil; this ayah gives its positive side directly, asking whether the recompense of excellence is anything but excellence (جزاء الإحسان إلا الإحسان).

luna: Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the wealth's prior source and temporary custody illuminate why the section's donor need not collect a human debt. | terra: People must spend from that over which God made them successors, so the human giver is a trustee of a prior gift rather than an original benefactor who can claim mastery.

luna: The section's debt world has a human creditor, while this ayah calls giving a good loan to God (يقرض الله قرضا حسنا) and promises its multiplication by Him. | terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward, transferring collection and increase away from claims on needy recipients.

luna: The section distinguishes giving from settling a human debt; this ayah places charity and a good loan to God together, with God multiplying the return, relocating the creditor relation. | terra: Male and female almsgivers are described as lending God a good loan that He multiplies, joining charity, debt, and divine recompense without making a human recipient indebted.

luna: This ayah names those who are stingy and turn away (يبخلون ... ومن يتول); it brings together the section's two roots for the withholding hand and the one who turns away. | terra: Those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and turn away meet the declaration that God is self-sufficient, again joining بخل and تولي around refusal to give.

luna: The verse says God's bounty is in His control and that He gives it to whom He wills; it anchors the section's “blessing as hand” image in God's unowed generosity. | terra: The repeated claim that bounty is in God's hand and He gives it as He wills identifies the ultimate hand behind every human benefaction.

luna: This ruling requires freeing a slave as expiation before a husband resumes marital relations after an oath; it shows the concrete release the section places at the center of its slavery image. | terra: Freeing a slave before the separated spouses touch is the required undoing of the offending declaration, another explicit emancipating hand.
luna: Neither wealth nor children will avail those facing God; this is another explicit boundary on the property that the section says cannot help its owner at the fall.
terra: The distribution rule prevents public wealth from circulating only among the rich, limiting the use of the giving hand to consolidate dependency and power.

luna: The Helpers give the emigrants priority over themselves even in hardship, and the verse says those protected from their own avarice succeed; it shows the freedom on the far side of the section's closed hand. | terra: The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite need and are protected from their own avarice, showing the opened hand overcoming inner grasping.
terra: Enemies would stretch their hands and tongues toward believers with harm, another specific reversal of the hand that ought to give.

luna: The passage calls faith and striving a trade that saves from painful punishment; this makes explicit the spiritual-exchange language behind the section's giver who acts for the Lord's face. | terra: The saving faith and expenditure that follow are introduced as a commerce, a divine transaction rather than leverage over recipients.
luna: The next ayah specifies that this trade involves striving with wealth and lives in God's way; it gives the concrete expenditure behind 61:10's image of trade.
luna: The next ayah names forgiveness and gardens as the reward for the trade introduced in 61:10 and specified by spending wealth in 61:11; it gives the divine return behind that exchange.
terra: The hypocrites propose withholding support until the Messenger's companions disperse, displaying the giving hand used as a means of control.

luna: Believers are told to spend from God's provision before death arrives, when a person will wish for delay; this makes the section's useless wealth at the fall an urgent reason to give. | terra: At death a person asks for delay in order to give charity, when the hand can no longer defer its release of wealth.

luna: Believers are told to spend for their own good and guard against their own miserliness; the section's stingy hand is thus a loss to its holder, not a debt avoided. | terra: The command to spend for one's own good is paired with protection from avarice, locating the decisive struggle inside the hand that gives or holds.

luna: This ayah again calls giving to God a good loan and promises its return multiplied; it clarifies that the section's release from human indebtedness can coexist with trust in God's recompense. | terra: Lending God a good loan brings multiplication and forgiveness, again replacing a human debt bond with divine repayment.
terra: The question who could provide if God withheld His provision exposes the human hand's dependence on a prior divine opening.
terra: The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them, using control of the harvest to close every requesting hand.
terra: After the garden is destroyed, its owners call themselves deprived, reversing the positions of those who denied the poor in 68:24.
terra: The repeated question about a wage and an overwhelming debt again defines guidance as a benefit without collection from its recipients.

luna: The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him (ما أغنى عني ماليه); this is the section's claim about wealth at the moment of collapse in another voice. | terra: The condemned person says that his wealth did not avail him, a direct parallel to the section's wealth failing its owner at the fall.
terra: The condemned person's authority has vanished, completing 69:28's failed wealth with the collapse of the power that wealth was supposed to secure.
terra: The fire calls the person who turned his back, linking the section's turning-away root with the fate of the closed hand.
terra: The one called by the fire gathered and withheld wealth, completing in 70:17-18 the sequence of turning away, accumulation, and refusal to give.
terra: The human being is introduced as anxiously grasping, the disposition from which the next verses derive withholding and the disciplined giver's exception.
terra: Distress makes the anxious person fretful, completing the fear-driven posture that becomes withholding when good arrives in 70:21.
terra: When good touches the anxious human he becomes مَنُوعًا, withholding it in the exact motion of the section's closing hand.

luna: The verse says a known share is kept in the wealth of those who pray; it presents provision for others as part of possessing wealth, not a favor that creates a personal debt. | terra: The worshippers recognize a fixed right in their wealth, denying that what leaves the giver's hand is merely optional leverage over another.

luna: The next ayah identifies the recipients of that share as the petitioner and deprived person; it completes 70:24's claim with the two hands that meet in the section's scene. | terra: That recognized right belongs to the asker and deprived person, supplying the recipient's outstretched hand for the wealth named in 70:24.

luna: After commanding prayer and zakat, this ayah asks believers to lend God a good loan; its divine recipient gives the section's no-human-debt gift a distinct, promised return. | terra: The command to give zakat and lend God a good loan joins obligatory giving to the divine debtor metaphor without burdening a human recipient.

luna: The section's listed dictionary wording for تمنن is giving while seeking an increase; this command forbids that transactional hand, matching the giver who seeks the Lord's face rather than more from people. | terra: وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving or recounting favor in order to gain more, the direct prohibition of an interested benefaction.

luna: The section's hand reaches outward to give; these people feed the poor, orphan, and captive out of love for the food, with the next ayah stating their no-recompense motive. | terra: They feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite love of the food; 76:9 supplies their refusal of repayment or thanks.

luna: The section's giver acts for the Lord's face without repaying a human hand; these feeders say they seek neither recompense nor thanks (لا نريد منكم جزاء ولا شكورا), making that motive explicit. | terra: The feeders say that they act only for God's face and want neither جَزَاءً nor thanks from the recipients, the closest parallel to giving without repaying or creating a human claim.
luna: The section identifies the turning-away root and the asking hand; here the addressed figure turns away as a visitor arrives, placing refusal beside a person who has come seeking attention.
luna: This ayah identifies the visitor as a blind man; it supplies the human need behind the turning-away in 80:1, though he comes seeking attention rather than a stated monetary gift.

luna: The arriving man's possible self-purification is raised here; it meets the section's donor who gives wealth to purify himself, while 80:2 identifies the visitor whose potential benefit was overlooked.

luna: The visitor might take heed and benefit from a reminder; this ayah gives a possible outcome for the seeker whose purification is raised in 80:3, echoing the section's concern with the one who fears and believes.
luna: This passage turns to the one who sees himself as self-sufficient (استغنى), the same posture named in the section's miser, and shows whom the addressed figure favors.
luna: The addressed figure attends to the self-sufficient man; after 80:5 identifies his posture, this ayah shows the social preference opposite the section's open hand to a needy recipient.

luna: The verse says the addressed figure is not responsible if the self-sufficient man does not purify himself; it qualifies 80:6's attention to him, while the section grounds purification in the giver's own act rather than a return extracted from someone else.
luna: The person who comes striving (يسعى) is the other side of the section's divided striving; this ayah introduces the seeker whose fear is named in 80:9.
luna: This ayah says the striving visitor is fearful; it echoes the section's giver who fears God, and 80:8 supplies the distinct act of striving.
luna: The addressed figure is distracted from the striving visitor; this completes the turning-away scene begun in 80:1 and contrasts with the section's attention to giving and striving.
luna: This ayah says the one who purifies himself succeeds; it makes explicit the self-purification named in the section's description of the giver's wealth.

luna: The person treats abundant provision as proof that God has honored him; this begins the passage's rebuke of reading wealth as self-sufficiency, which 89:17-20 connects to neglect of the vulnerable and love of wealth.

luna: When provision is restricted, the person calls it humiliation; beside 89:15, this shows the mistaken reading of wealth and scarcity that the passage answers with duties toward the orphan and poor.

luna: The passage rebukes people for not honoring the orphan; this is a concrete failure of the giving hand to the vulnerable, rather than a lack of wealth alone. | terra: Failure to honor the orphan begins a sequence in which love of wealth blocks obligations to vulnerable recipients.

luna: The passage adds that they do not encourage feeding the poor; this follows the failure to honor the orphan and names another recipient of the section's charitable hand. | terra: People do not urge one another to feed the poor, a communal version of the hand withheld from need.

luna: The people consume inheritance greedily; this is a concrete wrongful taking of another's due, matching the section's secondary sense of reaching for what is not one's right. | terra: Greedily consuming inheritance shows the taking hand alongside the refusal to feed described in 89:18.

luna: The passage says people love wealth intensely; this gives the inward attachment behind the section's miserly hand a direct formulation. | terra: Intense love of wealth names the attachment that closes the hand throughout the preceding sequence.

luna: A speaker boasts that he has spent abundant wealth (أهلكت مالا لبدا); the next ascent passage names freeing a slave and feeding the hungry, distinguishing display of expenditure from the section's beneficial open hand. | terra: The boast of having consumed abundant wealth presents expenditure as self-display, a plausible counter-image to giving solely for God's face.

luna: The section develops slavery as the most severe bond in the gift world; this ayah names freeing a neck (فك رقبة) as a concrete step on the difficult ascent. | terra: فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes freeing a neck itself the steep moral ascent, directly realizing the section's slave working to unbind his neck.

luna: The ascent continues with feeding during a day of hunger (في يوم ذي مسغبة); after 90:13 names freeing a slave, this row adds the costly provision that follows it. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger continues the steep ascent whose first definition in 90:13 is freeing a neck, joining emancipation to an opened provision hand.

luna: The next detail of the ascent is feeding an orphan who is a relative (يتيما ذا مقربة); it specifies a recipient of the section's giving hand, following 90:14's hunger scene. | terra: The orphaned relative is the first specified recipient of the feeding in 90:14, distinguishing this ayah's contribution from the act and from the next recipient.

luna: The ascent also reaches a poor person in distress (مسكينا ذا متربة); this row specifies another recipient, completing the acts listed after 90:13's freeing of a slave. | terra: The destitute person in the dust is the second specified recipient, completing the passage's movement from freeing a slave to relieving acute need.
luna: The verse says the soul succeeds when purified; it clarifies that the section's giving wealth to purify oneself concerns moral purification of the self.
terra: The Lord will give the Prophet until he is satisfied, presenting divine giving as the source of contentment rather than a human debt relation.
terra: The command not to oppress the orphan precedes the command about the asker, extending restraint from the refusing hand to another dependent person.

luna: The command not to repel a petitioner (السائل فلا تنهر) directly answers the section's dictionary scene of someone asking people with an outstretched palm. | terra: The command not to repel the asker governs the very begging hand developed by the section.
terra: The Prophet is told to speak of his Lord's نِعْمَة, locating favor in God beside the command concerning the asker in 93:10.
luna: This ayah says the human being transgresses; 96:7 gives the reason as seeing himself self-sufficient, matching the section's self-sufficient miser as the moral danger.
luna: The section describes the miser as one who considers himself self-sufficient; this verse uses the same self-sufficiency wording for the person whose false independence leads to transgression.
terra: The person who gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it embodies the grasping hand that converts possession into a continuing account.
terra: His belief that wealth will make him immortal states the false security behind the accumulation in 104:2 and the wealth that cannot save in the section.
terra: The accumulator is thrown into the Crusher, completing the reversal in which gathered wealth cannot prevent the owner's fall.
terra: Driving away the orphan supplies the bodily rejection whose next verse becomes refusal to encourage feeding the poor.
terra: Failure even to urge feeding the poor makes withholding visible as a social act rather than a private grip on wealth.
terra: Withholding ٱلْمَاعُونَ closes the hand even against small, ordinary assistance, a miniature form of the section's grasping palm.
terra: God's gift of abundance to the Prophet is a compact instance of the prior divine hand behind all subsequent human giving.
terra: The perishing of Abu Lahab's two hands makes the hand itself answer for what it grasped and performed.
terra: His wealth and acquisitions do not avail him, completing the ruined hands of 111:1 and closely echoing wealth that cannot save when one falls.
